Affiliation:: School of Biological Sciences, University of Oklahoma
Techniques Used: Grayscale morphology (including erosion, dilation, opening, closing, and top-hat transform)
Threshold Value of Efficiency (TVOE) method (including an improved slope-based method)
Data & Platforms: Köppen and Geiger's climate classification map
Tree height data (Global Land Analysis and Discovery)
Application Areas: Heat Governance and Public Health Policy
Key Research Thinking Patterns: Multi-Scale and Comparative Analysis: Investigating phenomena across different spatial scales, timeframes, or resolutions to identify scale-dependent effects and spatial non-stationarity. (e.g., Comparing the effect of urban form on LST at block vs. grid scales, analyzing greenspace impacts at "internal" vs. "surrounding" LCZ scales, and assessing park cooling effects using 30m vs. downscaled 10m data).

Explainable AI for Non-Linear Insights: Employing machine learning models to capture complex, non-linear relationships and using explainability methods to interpret model outputs. (e.g., Using an XGBoost-SHAP framework to move beyond simple correlation and identify specific LST response thresholds, such as a cooling effect when SHDI exceeds 0.65 or a warming effect when building density exceeds 20% ).

Integration of Standardized Frameworks: Applying established classification schemes to create a consistent basis for analyzing and comparing environmental data across diverse geographies. (e.g., Adopting the Local Climate Zone (LCZ) framework to categorize urban forms for thermal analysis and using the Thermal Condition Index (TCI) to enable a standardized comparison of thermal stress across 1,469 cities globally ).

Methodological Critique and Scalable Algorithm Development: Identifying limitations in existing data or methods (like data resolution or computational cost) and developing novel, efficient algorithms for large-scale application. (e.g., Critiquing how low-resolution LST data causes a "systematic overestimation" of park cooling effects, and developing the novel, sample-free STEM-OP method to efficiently extract single-tree data at a national scale using only RGB images).
Summary Description: Dr. Xiangming Xiao specializes in Remote Sensing, Environmental Science, and Ecology, exploring their interplay in urban climatology and large-scale vegetation mapping. Based at the University of Oklahoma, his research examines the urban thermal environment, using frameworks like Local Climate Zones (LCZs) to assess urban form's impact on Land Surface Temperature (LST) and investigating methodological biases in remote sensing studies. He also develops and supervises novel, large-scale vegetation mapping techniques, including single-tree extraction from sub-meter imagery. He consistently contributes to supervision, methodology, and validation, applying advanced models like XGBoost-SHAP and GWR to diverse satellite datasets (e.g., Landsat, ECOSTRESS, TCI).
